extracted.intended_audience: readers and researchers interested in the history and practice of advertising (historians, advertisers, general readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative principles and recurring practices for writing and placing advertisements, illustrated by 18th–19th century examples and author commentary. Focuses on ad copy elements, commercial practices (rates, circulation, agencies), and common anti-patterns (quackery, hyperbole).

rubrics_metrics.name: Terms of Payment
rubrics_metrics.description: One half the sum down, and the other half on the delivery of the articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state payment terms in the advertisement (deposit and balance on delivery). Example appears verbatim in Andrew Smith's advertisement as a standard transactional term.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of wares/services offered
rubrics_metrics.description: Give a clear inventory or list of goods: e.g., 'loaf-bread, crackers, pilot-bread, fresh rusks, &c. &c.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertise specific items available to inform customers of stock and scope of service. The baker's ad opens with a straightforward list of wares before other commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of payment expectations / request for prompt payment
rubrics_metrics.description: On his part nothing shall be left undone to give complete satisfaction to his customers, and in return he expects them to pay punctually when their bills are presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ads to set expectations about payment behaviour (request immediate payment, ask debtors to settle) — both to encourage prompt settlement and to signal business standards. Examples include appeals tied to the advertiser's travel or ill health.

rubrics_metrics.name: House rules and behavioral expectations (boarding ads)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for boarders (e.g., 'to bed at nine o'clock without a pipe or cigar', 'rise in time to wash their faces and comb their heads', 'pay their board weekly, monthly, or quarterly').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boarding-house advertisements often enumerate precise behavioural rules and expectations; including them screens applicants and sets the household tone. The Old McCalla example lists prohibitions and punctual payment terms as part of the ad copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear pricing and accommodation details
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide explicit prices and details of facilities: e.g., 'Board and Lodging $5 00 | Board $4 00', 'Six NEW rooms, furnished with beds — the BEST in town'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State rates and what is included (rooms, furnishings, branch houses) so potential customers can compare and decide quickly. Thompson's Two-Bit House shows direct pricing and facility claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sensational/ornate descriptive copy (property/auction ads)
rubrics_metrics.description: Highly picturesque, poetic description of a property: e.g., 'Streams of sparkling gladness (thick with trout) dance through this wilderness of beauty... The ever-green sighs as the evening zephyr flits through its shadowy bosom...' (N.B. This angel goes with the place.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ornate, emotional description can attract attention and create desire, but the author notes it can be excessive or absurd ('this one had shot his bolt'), implying a risk of undermining credibility if overdone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of current events or sensational news as advertising hook
rubrics_metrics.description: Tie products to news events or sensational stories: e.g., the Fort Sumter parody leading to 'Exquisite Card Photographs' sold at 28 cents per copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leveraging topical events or sensational headlines draws reader attention and can boost sales of related products (photographs, prints). The example shows using a dramatic news-style opening to promote goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-form persuasive structure for medical/tonic ads
rubrics_metrics.description: Extended preamble, 'Symptoms', 'Important Facts', 'Reasons why Dr Hamilton is successful', and numerous testimonials culminating in exhortations to write to the Doctor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent-medicine ads commonly used long, structured narratives: define symptoms, assert 'important facts', list reasons for efficacy, produce testimonials, and finish with a direct call to action. The author highlights this as a widespread and effective (if often deceptive) formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of testimonials and dramatic case histories
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous testimonials with sensational headings and asserted cures (e.g., 'gained twenty pounds in three months').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testimonials are used to lend credibility and evoke emotional response; the author warns about their inconsequence and potential for fabrication ('IS ALL THIS TRUE?' test shows testimonials may be untrustworthy). Verify claims where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outlandish claims and anecdotal 'tests' (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extraordinary product tests and claims: 'Take a hew or a ram, drive a nail through its skull, brains and tongue... it will directly stop the blood and cure the wound in eight or nine minutes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such implausible demonstrations signal quackery. The text uses these as examples of absurd claims that should be treated skeptically; advertisers should avoid making physically impossible or easily falsifiable claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measures to prevent counterfeiting / mark of authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Products and bottles 'are sealed up with this seal (A. K. Balsam) to prevent counterfeits.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use seals, distinctive packaging, or marks to assure buyers of authenticity and to deter counterfeits. The Riga Balsam ad explicitly claims sealed packaging as a safeguard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour and first-person testimonial style for local goods
rubrics_metrics.description: Engaging, humorous first-person endorsements (e.g., 'My wife had an ulcer... Until I used Wolcott's Pain Paint... It has done the work complete In less than one month').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Witty, conversational first-person copy can humanize ads for local businesses and hotels; the Pain Paint example shows such copy can be entertaining and persuasive when tied to a named proprietor and address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution/warning notices to protect reputation and customers
rubrics_metrics.description: 'we hereby caution all persons that we are not responsible for any of his acts. He is in no way connected with us, but is a perfect dead beat...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish clear warnings about impostors or unauthorized agents to protect customers and the firm's reputation. The 'Dead beat' caution exemplifies public repudiation of fraudulent representatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pricing per line and the importance of cost vs. circulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising rates given (e.g., Harper's inner pages: '1 dollar 50 cents per line'; Paris journals: 'one franc per line' or 'one franc fifty centimes per line').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertisers must weigh per-line costs against the paper's circulation and audience. The book notes Harper's high rates and implies advertisers should judge value for money given reach and readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication value and advertiser trust (circulation credibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'It is hard to make advertisers believe that it is worth while paying for a notice in a paper which is itself not worth paying for...'; Scotchman's scheme 'He guarantees to the advertiser a circulation of five thousand copies.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A publication's perceived value and verifiable circulation are key to attracting advertisers. Schemes promising circulation guarantees should be examined (example: Scotchman's plan includes a stated guarantee and cost breakdown). Advertisers are reluctant to pay for ads in publications that lack perceived or demonstrated readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of advertising agencies / column-farming model
rubrics_metrics.description: Parisian journals 'did not themselves deal with the advertisers, but farmed out their columns at so much a year to advertising establishments or agencies.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers may outsource ad sales to agencies which set rates and control column space; advertisers should be aware of intermediaries and their pricing practices when placing ads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local/customary phrasing and cultural references (copy tone)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ad copy often employs local idioms and cultural references (e.g., 'Hi-you Muck-a-muck' from Chinook language, Australian threats 'you will receive a tight cravat under the gallows by Jack Ketch').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tone and idiom can be tailored to local audiences to achieve familiarity and impact, but some phrasing may be culturally insensitive or offensive by modern standards; advertisers historically used regional color freely.
